notes: Shareholder deadlock and debenture enforcement; payment, extension and authority issues are fully determined.

enrichment.short_title: Fusion v Pertemps: debenture acceleration and restraint of receiver appointment
key_facts: Fusion Interactive sought to restrain Venture Investment Placement (Pertemps) from appointing administrative receivers under a debenture securing a loan and management services fees.
A £23,500 invoice for October 2004 management services was due on 31 December 2004; non-payment would accelerate the entire loan under clause 8 of the debenture.
Fusion claimed a cheque had been prepared but not sent before Pertemps staff left its Leeds offices; Pertemps argued deliberate withholding and no set-off under clause 16.
Parallel winding-up petitions, shareholder deadlock and disputes over authority to sue complicated the satellite application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Final determination of an application by order to restrain receiver appointment after interim injunctions and a part-heard fact-finding hearing in the Chancery Division.
enrichment.outcome: Final injunction granted against receiver appointment; payment was made within time under an earlier demand letter and there was no debenture default or loan acceleration.
enrichment.ratio: A creditor's written demand extending payment time can vary the due date under a debenture; where a cheque for a secured debt was in the creditor's employees' possession but not presented because they left it behind, the debtor is not in default; proceedings to challenge enforcement may be authorised despite board deadlock where the creditor treated the claimant's solicitors as acting for the company.
legal_issues: Whether the £23,500 management services invoice was paid by 31 December 2004
Whether the 31 December 2004 demand extended time for payment to 4 January 2005
Whether Messrs Seear and Hopkins had authority to bring proceedings on behalf of Fusion
Construction of debenture clauses on default, acceleration and exclusion of set-off
linked_authorities: Mitchell & Hobbs (UK) Ltd v Mill [1996] 2 BCLC 102
Nova (Jersey) Knit Ltd v Kammgarn Spinnerei GmbH [1977] 2 All ER 463
Siebe Gorman & Co Ltd v Pneupac Ltd [1982] 1 WLR 185

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings on payment and extension issues and clear final injunctive relief.

notes: Unsafe conviction appeal; undisclosed interpreter suspension is clearly decisive.

enrichment.short_title: R v Cakir: blackmail conviction quashed over interpreter suspension
key_facts: Huseyin Cakir was convicted of blackmail after demanding payment from Halil Esmene in a dry-cleaning partnership dispute.
Covert recordings of the visit were interpreted by Mr Duzen, who emphatically testified the appellant said 'You will not remain in life'.
Defence interpreter Miss Simsek disputed any death threat; the appellant denied threatening to kill.
Mr Duzen had been suspended from the Metropolitan Police interpreters list in March 2004 for over-claiming expenses and unsupervised statements, but counsel were not told.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge following trial at Inner London Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed; no retrial ordered given time already served in custody.
enrichment.ratio: Where a prosecution interpreter's evidence on a disputed death threat was central and emphatic and he had prayed in aid his integrity, non-disclosure of his suspension for integrity-related matters could have significantly affected the jury and renders the conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of the interpreter's suspension affected the safety of the conviction
Whether the disputed death threat was crucial or the offence was already complete
Whether the co-defendant's conviction showed the jury disregarded the final threat
Whether a retrial was in the interests of justice

confidence.notes: Central evidential issue and appellate reasoning on safety are explicit.

notes: VWF quantum test case; apportionment methodology and Allen principles are thoroughly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Rugby Joinery v Whitfield: apportionment of VWF damages after employer negligence
key_facts: Mrs Whitfield contracted vibration white finger after decades using vibratory tools at Rugby Joinery's Doncaster factory.
Liability had been established on appeal because the employer failed to monitor symptoms and warn her after 1991/92.
General damages of £15,000 and special damages of £1,900 were agreed; the judge deducted one-fifth for non-negligent exposure.
The defendant argued for straight time-based apportionment of exposure years rather than assessment of worsening beyond the first symptomatic stage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Sheffield County Court quantum assessment following reinstatement of liability by the Court of Appeal in Doherty v Rugby Joinery.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; award of £13,520 upheld as within acceptable margin though reasoning could have been clearer.
enrichment.ratio: In VWF cases damages should reflect worsening attributable to negligent post-symptom exposure, deducting compensation for the first stage and inevitable deterioration; straight line time apportionment is unrealistic where symptoms appeared only after many years of earlier exposure.
legal_issues: Whether the judge failed to account for inevitable deterioration after cessation of exposure
Whether a £3,000 deduction was too small
Whether time-based apportionment under Allen was required
When the employer should have discovered symptoms and warned the claimant
linked_authorities: Doherty v Rugby Joinery (UK) Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 147
Allen v British Rail Engineering Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 242
Armstrong v British Coal Corporation (No 2) (31 July 1998, unreported)

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of quantum methodology though some judge's reasoning required interpretation.

notes: Fresh evidence appeal on fingerprint provenance; Murat evidence rejected and appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: R v Barnes: fingerprint lift provenance appeal dismissed
key_facts: Barnes was convicted in 1997 of robbing Allan and Audrey Pickles and inflicting GBH on Mr Pickles at their Whitefield home.
Lift 6, a fingerprint from the small bedroom door, and lift 7 from a bottle shard linked the appellant to the scene.
Years later arboriculturalist Mr Murat compared wood-grain patterns on lift 6 with the preserved door and concluded it could not have come from that door.
Multiple fingerprint and forensic experts had previously declined to undertake such a comparison.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on fresh evidence under section 23 Criminal Appeal Act 1968 heard de bene esse with additional Crown witnesses.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Murat's evidence lacked sufficient weight and admissible expert status to render the 1997 verdict unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: An arboriculturalist lacks expertise to compare fingerprint lift background striations with a door surface years later; incomplete lifts reflecting powder, pressure and contaminants cannot reliably be matched to wood-grain, and alleged police planting faced overwhelming coincidences including lift 7 from a taxi-linked bottle shard.
legal_issues: Whether Murat's evidence was capable of belief and admissible under section 23
Whether lift 6 was obtained from the Pickles bedroom door on 5 August 1995
Whether wood-grain comparison could exclude the lift's provenance
Whether the jury's verdict was unsafe in light of fresh evidence

confidence.notes: Extensive reasoning on admissibility, weight and safety of verdict is clearly recorded.

notes: Section 459 permission applications; selective grants on forgery and exclusion grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Blackmore v Richardson: permission to appeal on unfair prejudice petition
key_facts: Mr Blackmore petitioned under section 459 alleging unfair prejudice in Capital Cabs Limited, a quasi-partnership taxi business.
Richardson and Wheeler secretly negotiated sale of their shares to Carl Cummings and Supatax 2000 Ltd while excluding Blackmore.
Blackmore had forged a letter in November 2001; the judge found exclusion from management and secret share negotiations unfair.
The judge ordered Richardson and Wheeler to buy Blackmore's shares after a bitter multi-party trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal from HHJ Wyn Williams QC's section 459 judgment in the Mercantile Court.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on grounds relating to forgery altering quasi-partnership, clean hands, and exclusion finding; otherwise refused including Cummings and most Capital Cabs grounds except £60,000 payment-out order.
enrichment.ratio: Share dealings may form part of a company's affairs where associated with board meetings and conduct of company business; a petitioner's forgery may arguably alter a quasi-partnership and the clean hands doctrine in section 459 may require reconsideration after O'Neill v Phillips.
legal_issues: Whether share sale negotiations were affairs of the company under section 459
Whether the petitioner's forgery unilaterally ended the quasi-partnership
Whether clean hands bars equitable relief under section 459
Whether the judge erred in finding Blackmore was excluded from the company
linked_authorities: In re London School of Electronics Ltd [1976] 1 Ch 211

confidence.notes: Permission decisions are explicit though full merits remain for the appeal hearing.

notes: Civil restraint order confirmation after 135-page representations; brief court judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Forrester Ketley v Brent: civil restraint order confirmed
key_facts: Mr Brent's appeals against Forrester Ketley & Co were dismissed and a civil restraint order made on 1 March 2005.
He submitted 135 pages of further representations challenging the order and re-arguing the underlying dispute.
The court had previously found he had mounted numerous applications and appeals that were totally without merit.
Brent alleged a cabal of Lord Justices and sought to choose his judges; he cited stress-related heart condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court determination following post-judgment representations on whether to discharge a civil restraint order made after appeal dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Civil restraint order of 1 March 2005 confirmed until 1 March 2007; defendant to pay £18,400 costs.
enrichment.ratio: A litigant may not pick judges or persist in wholly inappropriate and disproportionate proceedings; extensive meritless submissions reinforce the need for a civil restraint order to protect claimants, and ECHR applications are not barred by such an order.
legal_issues: Whether the civil restraint order should be discharged
Whether Brent had sufficient notice before the order was made
Whether the order infringed his Human Rights Act rights
Whether his health prevented him conducting proceedings

confidence.notes: Short but clear confirmation of the restraint order and refusal of discharge.

notes: Cooksley sentencing appeal; custodial term and disqualification reduced on mitigation.

enrichment.short_title: R v Dunne: reduced sentence for death by dangerous driving
key_facts: The 16-year-old appellant took his grandmother's car without consent and drove uninsured and unlicensed with three passengers, none belted.
He entered a bend at about 50 mph in a 30 mph limit, lost control and rolled the car, killing Nicholas Llewellyn and seriously injuring Joe Lane.
He fled the scene and was arrested three days later; the jury rejected his account of an oncoming car.
He was sentenced to four years' detention under section 91 and disqualified for eight years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge following conviction at Guildford Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; custodial term reduced from four years to three years and disqualification from eight to five years with extended retest.
enrichment.ratio: Death by dangerous driving with one fatality and serious permanent injury to another falls in intermediate Cooksley culpability; strong personal mitigation including youth, learning difficulties and troubled home life can justify reduction below an otherwise appropriate four-year term, and disqualification should follow Cooksley starting points adjusted for illegal driving history.
legal_issues: Whether four years' section 91 detention was manifestly excessive
Whether eight years' disqualification was manifestly excessive
Application of R v Cooksley guidelines
Weight of age, good character and psychological mitigation

confidence.notes: Sentencing reasoning and precise reductions are clearly stated.

notes: Limitation appeal on continuing tort argument; Phonographic distinguished and claims dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Iqbal v Legal Services Commission: limitation of solicitor's tort claims
key_facts: Mr Iqbal and his partner's Bradford firm claimed the Legal Aid Board wrongly withheld payments from spring 1997, contributing to the firm's collapse.
Judicial review proceedings were compromised in November 1997; the firm was intervened in November 1997 and wound up in 2002.
The liquidator assigned causes of action to Iqbal who issued proceedings in October 2003 for breach of statutory duty and misfeasance in public office.
All pleaded wrongful acts occurred before October 1997 and material damage arose before that date, including staff redundancies in May 1997.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Mercantile Court decision that assigned tort claims were statute-barred under the six-year limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; neither breach of statutory duty nor misfeasance constituted a continuing tort giving fresh causes of action after October 1997.
enrichment.ratio: Where a single wrongful withholding causes a chain of damage beginning before the limitation date, later catastrophic consequences do not revive the cause of action; section 6 Legal Aid Act 1988 breach and misfeasance here were not continuing wrongs like repeated toxic emissions, and Phonographic Performance is distinguishable where no post-limitation breaches were pleaded.
legal_issues: When causes of action for breach of section 6 Legal Aid Act 1988 accrued
Whether withholding legal aid money was a continuing tort after October 1997
Whether misfeasance maliciously intended to close the firm within the limitation period
Application of Khan v Falvey and Phonographic Performance Ltd v DTI

Office for the Supervision of Solicitors
linked_authorities: Phonographic Performance Ltd v Department of Trade and Industry [2004] 1 WLR 2893
Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 3) [2003] 2 AC 1

notes: Complex reinsurance stay application; jurisdiction clause and case management discretion fully analysed.

enrichment.short_title: KCM v Coromin: stay of Part 20 reinsurance proceedings refused
key_facts: Konkola Copper Mines claimed indemnity for losses from a 2001 rock and mud avalanche at its Zambian Nchanga copper mine that killed ten miners.
Claims were pursued against Bermudian captive Coromin under an all-risks policy and against Zambian local insurers under specified perils including collapse.
Coromin brought Part 20 proceedings against English and European reinsurers; reinsurers sought a stay pending Zambian coverage proceedings.
Reinsurance followed specified-perils KCM wording with a Zambian law and jurisdiction clause; the central issue was whether the loss was a covered collapse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application to stay Part 20 proceedings against reinsurers pending determination of coverage issues affecting their liability.
enrichment.outcome: Stay application dismissed; Part 20 proceedings against reinsurers should continue in England with Aon joined to avoid conflicting decisions.
enrichment.ratio: Although reinsurers had contractual entitlement to Zambian jurisdiction and the evidential centre of gravity on collapse coverage lay in Zambia, justice favoured a single English tribunal deciding issues between KCM, Coromin, reinsurers and brokers and avoiding inconsistent judgments likely to complete before any Zambian trial.
legal_issues: Whether Part 20 proceedings against reinsurers should be stayed pending Zambian proceedings
Effect of Zambian law and jurisdiction clauses in reinsurance
Whether coverage turned on all-risks or specified collapse perils
Case management under CPR overriding objective and risk of conflicting decisions

confidence.notes: Discretionary outcome and reasoning are explicit though coverage merits remain undecided.

notes: Article 6 naval court-martial appeal; prosecuting authority reporting practice held incompatible.

enrichment.short_title: R v Stow: naval court-martial conviction quashed for Article 6 breach
key_facts: Operator Mechanic Stow pleaded guilty at a naval court-martial to drunkenness and insubordinate language and was dismissed and detained for 42 days.
Before plea he argued the naval Prosecuting Authority lacked Article 6 independence; the judge advocate rejected a stay as beyond his power.
Commander Crozier, the naval Prosecuting Authority, was appraised within the service on prosecution performance including successful case outcomes.
Unlike Army and RAF counterparts he was reported upon, not in his final posting, and held junior rank.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge after refusal of a service petition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed; naval Prosecuting Authority at the time lacked sufficient objective safeguards of independence and impartiality.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 requires the prosecuting authority in service proceedings to appear free from improper pressure; appraisal within the Royal Navy commenting on prosecution outcomes, combined with scope for promotion and relatively junior rank, meant an objective observer could doubt Commander Crozier's independence despite legal qualifications and CPS-style codes.
legal_issues: Whether the naval Prosecuting Authority breached Article 6 independence requirements
Whether the judge advocate could stay proceedings as an abuse of process
Significance of service appraisal reports on prosecution performance
Comparison with Cooper and Grieves Strasbourg jurisprudence

confidence.notes: Article 6 analysis and quashing of conviction are clearly reasoned with detailed factual background.
